omnibus_nss.category: Seat booking · team project at CTU FEL
omnibus_nss.headline: Two passengers, one seat, no double booking
omnibus_nss.pitch: A bus booking system where you pick your seat on a plan of the coach. When two people grab the same seat at the same moment, only one of them gets it.
omnibus_nss.credit: Team semester project at CTU FEL by Mykhailo Plokhin and Ivan Shestachenko. A demo, not a real carrier.

overbooking.label: Double bookings
overbooking.note: The design target: the second booking is refused on the spot instead of a cleanup job fixing it later.

lock.label: Seat lock
lock.note: A PostgreSQL advisory lock on the trip and seat, taken before the seat is checked (ReservationPassengerRepository).

deploy.label: Runs on
deploy.note: Containers on a k3s cluster, at the address linked from this page.

problem.lede: Booking systems break exactly when two people want the same thing at the same time. That is also when the business earns money.
points: If the app reads a seat and then writes it, two requests can both see it free and both book it.
Overbooking is often repaired afterwards with a nightly job and an apology, instead of being impossible in the first place.
Passengers and dispatchers need different rights, not the same endpoint behind a different screen.

design.lede: One service owns reservations and nothing else writes a seat. A contested seat goes through one short transaction that holds a lock on that seat.

solutions.why: A seat is sold for a stretch of the route, and two bookings clash only where their stretches overlap. A unique key cannot express an overlap, so the schema alone would accept the second row. The lock turns check-then-insert into one step for that seat, and other seats keep booking in parallel.
The timetable, the seat map and the dispatcher only read. With a single writer, "one seat, one passenger" is a rule the system can actually check.
Spring Security resolves the role before the handler runs, so a dispatcher action cannot be reached from a passenger URL.

results.lede: Omnibus is a university project with a live demo, not a commercial service. Measured figures are checked in the code; a target is what it is designed for.

race.a: Passenger A books seat 12. The database locks that seat.
race.b: Passenger B asks for seat 12 at the same moment and waits for the lock.
race.c: A's booking commits. B is told the seat is taken, not double-booked.

boowie.headline: Books and audiobooks in one app, even offline
boowie.pitch: Reads EPUB, FB2 and PDF and plays MP3 and M4B audiobooks. Books stay on the phone and open without internet; the built-in store has 82 free books. Pages turn like paper, sounds play while you read, and the year in books comes as stories to share.
boowie.credit: Personal project by Mykhailo Plokhin. Installs from the browser on Android and iPhone.

formats.label: Formats
formats.note: EPUB, FB2, PDF, MP3 and M4B, plus ZIP archives of them.

store.label: Free books
store.note: Public-domain books in Russian and English in the built-in store, four of them audiobooks narrated with RHVoice.

offline.label: Works
offline.note: A service worker caches the app, and books are stored on the device.

sounds.label: Sounds for reading
sounds.note: Rain, a storm, a fireplace, the sea, a forest, a summer night and a train, synthesised on the device from noise, with no sound files.

achievements.label: Achievements
achievements.note: Badges with levels, two of them secret, worked out on the device from the reading statistics.

problem.lede: Most readers handle either text or audio, want an account, or break on real-life files: odd encodings, zipped folders, MP3s without chapters.
points: Russian FB2 files come in windows-1251 or koi8-r, often mislabelled.
An audiobook is usually a folder of files, or a ZIP made by the iPhone Files app.
Reading and listening to the same book means two positions to keep in step.

design.lede: Everything runs on the device; an account is optional and only carries the library and statistics to your other devices. Files go through the same parsers whether they come from the phone or the store; records go to IndexedDB, large files to the browser's private file system.

solutions.why: A book opens and reads without internet and without an account. Signing in is optional and only carries the library, places and statistics to your other devices.
An audiobook folder zipped on an iPhone can be gigabytes. Reading entries as a stream keeps them out of memory, including ZIP64 archives and Russian file names.

solutions.choice: Large files in the private file system
solutions.why: The Origin Private File System holds big files without the limits of older storage; older iOS Safari falls back to IndexedDB.

solutions.choice: One position for text and audio
solutions.why: When a book has an audio edition, switching maps the place by chapter and by how far into it you were.

Each sound is filtered noise plus small events, drops, crackles, waves, rail joints, rendered in a web worker into a loop of 20 to 40 seconds whose end fades into its start. Nothing to download, and it works offline.

solutions.choice: A page that folds where you hold it
solutions.why: The page bends along the line halfway between its corner and the finger, with its back and the fold's shadow drawn over the next page. Let go past a quarter and it turns; otherwise it falls back.

solutions.choice: Everything counted from one set of daily rows
solutions.why: The reading map, the achievements and the year in review are worked out from the same rows per day and book. Nothing extra is stored or synced, and every device of an account agrees.
A shared passage and the year's summary are drawn in a canvas and handed to the share sheet. They are not uploaded anywhere.

results.lede: Boowie is live: open it on a phone and add it to the home screen. Every figure here is checked in the code or on the live app.

updates.lede: Added in November: the things that make a reading app feel like a book. Pages turn like paper, sounds play while you read, a passage becomes a picture to share, and the reading adds up to a map, badges and a year told in stories.

pageTurn.title: Pages that turn like paper
pageTurn.body: Take a page by its edge and it bends where you hold it, its back and shadow showing. A swish, a rustle and a soft landing go with it, made on the spot from noise.

sounds.title: Sounds for reading
sounds.body: Rain, a storm, a fireplace, the sea, a forest, a summer night and a train. Drag a sound up to bring it in, mix several, and every book starts in silence.

select.title: A word explained, a passage shared
select.body: Select a word and its meaning opens over the page, from Wiktionary. Select a phrase and it becomes a picture: four looks, three shapes, drawn on the phone.

map.title: Reading map and statistics
map.body: Time listening and reading, pages, books and days in a row, for a week, a month or all time. The year shows as twelve calendars, each day shaded by its time with books.

achievements.title: Achievements
achievements.body: Seventeen badges with levels, from bronze to ruby, two of them secret. They come from the same statistics, so every device of an account agrees.

year.title: Your year in books

mixer.body: Four of the app's seven sounds, made in your browser from noise, the same idea as in Boowie: no sound files. Slide a sound to bring it in and set its level, and slide it back to take it away. They mix, so rain can go with the fireplace.
mixer.note: Nothing plays until you turn a sound up. A tap turns it on or off; leaving the page stops it.

morph.caption: Switch between reading and listening and you stay in the same place in the chapter.

wovie_next.headline: Find a film, keep a watchlist
wovie_next.pitch: A film catalogue with genres, TMDB ratings, favourites and watchlists, built to stay fast on top of a large third-party catalogue.
wovie_next.credit: Personal project by Mykhailo Plokhin. Work in progress.

route.label: Page change
route.note: The target for moving between pages, not measured yet.

revalidate.label: Catalogue refresh
revalidate.note: Catalogue pages are rendered once and refreshed every hour.

problem.lede: A film catalogue is mostly someone else's data. The work is keeping it fast and reliable when that source is slow or changes.
points: Fetching TMDB on every visit makes TMDB's bad day your bad day.
Rendering everything in the browser makes a slow phone wait for the first poster.
Watchlists belong to one person, so they cannot be cached like the catalogue.

design.lede: Catalogue pages render on the server and are cached for an hour. Only personal data, favourites and watchlists, reads the database.

solutions.choice: Cache catalogue pages for an hour
solutions.why: The catalogue is the same for everyone, so it is rendered once an hour instead of on every visit. If TMDB is down, visitors see slightly older data instead of an error.

solutions.choice: Film pages rendered on the server
solutions.why: Film pages, Top Rated and New Releases arrive as HTML, so a slow phone is not left waiting for JavaScript. The main browse page is still rendered in the browser. It is next on the list.

solutions.choice: The database only for personal data
solutions.why: Favourites and watchlists need real per-person reads; everything else stays out of the database.

results.lede: Wovie is a work in progress with a public demo, and its source is open.

jo_plokhina.category: Online store and stock system · client project
jo_plokhina.headline: From a paper notebook to one system
jo_plokhina.pitch: A family shoe business in Zhytomyr moves its stock, orders and delivery from a paper notebook into one system. Its first visible part is the online store, with stock in each market stall and size advice by foot length.
jo_plokhina.credit: Built by MIW Labs for the business. Stage 0 of 4 is done: the system is built and tested on demo data. Payments and Nova Poshta are stand-ins until real sales start.

race.label: Last pairs
race.note: In a test, 12 shoppers race for 4 pairs and exactly 4 orders go through.

tests.label: Automated tests
tests.note: 110 unit and integration tests and 30 end-to-end runs on a phone and a laptop, with accessibility checks.

locations.label: Places with stock
locations.note: Two market stalls and three garages in one stock table.

threats.label: Threats covered
threats.note: Each threat to stock, prices, payments and customer data has a written control and the place where it is tested.

problem.lede: The business sells women's shoes from two market stalls and three garages, often one pair per size. Everything known about stock and sales is in one paper notebook, so decisions are made from memory.
points: Nobody can see at a glance whether a size is in the other stall or in a garage.
Fit changes from model to model, and online a size number alone does not tell a buyer what will fit.
Purchasing goes by feel, and the notebook is the only copy of the data.

design.lede: One database holds the stock of all five places. The people who have the shoes in hand enter the changes; the website, delivery, payments, notifications and purchasing read the same numbers and keep no records of their own.

changes.after: On the website, in the back office and in the bot, for all five places at once
One tap on a phone updates the stock everywhere
The site reserves the pair, the waybill is created and its number goes to Viber
Entered on a phone, the pairs show on the site at once

changes.now: Summed up by hand from the notebook
changes.after: Sales and receipts exported from the database
Sales by size and a hint of what to restock
A list by phone number, with consent, and a message when her size is back

solutions.why: Stock lives in one database. The website, the back office, the bot and later the marketplaces read it and never keep their own count.
Stock rows are locked in a fixed order, so two orders for the last pair cannot both succeed. A test sends 12 shoppers after 4 pairs: exactly 4 orders go through.
The site suggests a size by foot length in each model. With the real catalogue come insoles measured per size, width and instep, and a note from the owner on how each model fits.

solutions.choice: Money only when the stock is right
solutions.why: The work goes in four stages with a gate between each. Buyers can pay online only after a stock-take shows the database matches the shelves.

solutions.choice: Simple for the people who use it
solutions.why: A phone, a couple of buttons, a Telegram bot. If something takes longer than a line in the notebook, the system is wrong.

stages.name: Foundation
stages.goal: The base to sell on: the store from the prototype in Ukrainian and English, stock for five places, orders without overselling, a back office with roles, 140 automated tests.

stages.name: Launch as a case
stages.goal: A live site with the real range and digital stock-keeping, without online payment: photos and insoles for 10 to 20 models, delivery, exchange and size pages, stock-takes from a phone.
stages.gate: Gate: a stock-take matches the database, and the payment provider is chosen.

stages.name: Real sales
stages.goal: An order goes from payment to waybill with no manual steps: payments and refunds, fiscal receipts, Nova Poshta, an orders screen, Viber messages for buyers and a Telegram bot for the owner.
stages.gate: Gate: orders run without manual steps, and there are two to three months of sales data.

stages.name: Automation and growth
stages.goal: Purchasing by data and new channels on the same database: restock hints by size, transfers with QR codes on the boxes, a customer list, a Made in Zhytomyr line, Prom and Rozetka.

results.lede: Stage 0 of 4 is done and checked by automated tests on GitHub. Success here means less routine and fewer lost sales, not just traffic. The baselines are taken in the first month of digital stock-keeping, so there are no target figures yet.

race.alt: Twelve shoppers race for four pairs and exactly four orders go through
race.a: Twelve shoppers press buy at the same moment, and four pairs are left.
race.b: Each order locks the stock rows it needs, always in the same order, so the orders queue instead of colliding.
race.c: Exactly four orders go through. The other eight see the pair is sold out, and no pair is sold twice.

fit.result: A {{foot}} cm foot takes size {{size}} in this model: its insole is {{insole}} cm.
fit.none: No size from 36 to 41 is long enough for this foot.
fit.note: The rule the shop uses: the smallest size whose insole is at least as long as the foot. A measured insole replaces the estimate.
